subtopic_detail: Back pain for two years that wakes a young man at four in the morning and eases with movement, with normal pelvic radiographs
stem:
You are the general physician seeing a 26 year old man referred with two years of lower back pain. He has been treated with physiotherapy and intermittent ibuprofen with partial benefit.

The pain wakes him at around four in the morning and he has to get out of bed and move about before he can settle. He has an hour of stiffness each morning before he loosens up, and the pain improves with exercise rather than rest. He had one episode of a painful red eye treated with steroid drops eighteen months ago. His father has psoriasis. On examination his lumbar flexion is reduced with a modified Schober measurement of 3.5 cm and there is tenderness over both sacroiliac joints. Plain radiographs of the pelvis are reported as showing normal sacroiliac joints. His C reactive protein is 14 mg/L (less than 5) and HLA-B27 is positive.

data_table.Examination: Reduced lumbar flexion with modified Schober measurement 3.5 cm, tenderness on direct pressure over both sacroiliac joints, chest expansion 4.5 cm, no peripheral joint swelling, no dactylitis, no psoriatic skin or nail changes, no enthesitis at the Achilles insertions
data_table.Investigations: Plain radiographs of the pelvis reported as normal sacroiliac joints, C reactive protein 14 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 28 mm/h (less than 15), HLA-B27 positive, full blood count within normal limits, rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibody negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the sacroiliac joints
options.rationale: Inflammatory back pain with a positive HLA-B27, raised inflammatory markers and a history of acute anterior uveitis points to axial spondyloarthritis, and magnetic resonance imaging detects active bone marrow oedema and structural change years before radiographic sacroiliitis appears. Normal radiographs do not exclude the diagnosis and identify only the non-radiographic form of the disease. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial spondyloarthritis position statement)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial spondyloarthritis position statement

options.text: Repeat plain radiographs of the pelvis in twelve months
options.rationale: Waiting for radiographic change means waiting years, during which inflammation continues and function declines, and a substantial proportion of patients never progress to radiographic sacroiliitis at all. Serial radiographs have a role in monitoring established structural disease rather than in making an early diagnosis. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial spondyloarthritis position statement)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial spondyloarthritis position statement

options.text: Computed tomography of the lumbar spine and sacroiliac joints
options.rationale: Computed tomography images cortical bone well and can show erosion or ankylosis but cannot demonstrate the active inflammation that establishes an early diagnosis, and it delivers a significant pelvic radiation dose to a young man. Its niche is where magnetic resonance imaging is contraindicated or where the structural anatomy is genuinely unclear. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial spondyloarthritis position statement)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial spondyloarthritis position statement

options.text: Dual energy X-ray absorptiometry of the spine and hip
options.rationale: Bone density measurement is relevant later, since axial inflammation and immobility cause secondary osteoporosis and vertebral fracture, but it does not address the diagnostic question in front of you. It becomes part of long term surveillance once the diagnosis is made. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial spondyloarthritis position statement)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial spondyloarthritis position statement

options.text: Nuclear medicine whole body bone scan with delayed images
options.rationale: Bone scintigraphy lacks both the sensitivity and the specificity needed at the sacroiliac joints, where degenerative change and normal variation produce comparable uptake. It is better suited to searching for occult fracture or metastatic disease. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Axial spondyloarthritis)

explanation.summary: Axial spondyloarthritis typically begins in the twenties and thirties yet the average delay from symptom onset to diagnosis in Australia remains several years, largely because clinicians wait for radiographic sacroiliitis that may take a decade to appear or never appear at all. The features that identify inflammatory rather than mechanical back pain are onset before 45, duration beyond three months, morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes, improvement with exercise but not with rest, night pain in the second half of the night forcing the patient to get up, and a good response to non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Supporting features are the extra-articular manifestations that patients often do not connect with their back, including acute anterior uveitis, psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease, together with a family history, a raised C reactive protein and HLA-B27 positivity. Magnetic resonance imaging of the sacroiliac joints is the investigation that closes the diagnostic gap, and treatment begins with regular non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and structured exercise, escalating to tumour necrosis factor or interleukin 17 inhibitors for persistently active disease, since conventional agents such as methotrexate do not work for axial disease.
key_points: Night pain in the second half of the night with morning stiffness defines inflammatory back pain
Normal radiographs do not exclude the diagnosis and define the non-radiographic form
Uveitis, psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease are supporting features
Magnetic resonance imaging detects active inflammation years before radiographic change
Methotrexate is ineffective for axial disease; biologic therapy is the escalation
explanation.pearls: HLA-B27 is carried by roughly 8 per cent of the Australian population and only a small minority of carriers develop disease, so it is a supporting feature within a clinical picture and never a screening test; ordering it in mechanical back pain generates far more false alarms than diagnoses.

sources.label: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial spondyloarthritis position statement

subtopic_detail: Joint aches and tiredness in a man whose ferritin is 1250 with a transferrin saturation of 68 per cent and two copies of the common iron loading variant
stem:
You are the general physician seeing a 48 year old man referred after abnormal iron studies were found during investigation of six months of fatigue and aching in both second and third metacarpophalangeal joints.

He drinks four standard drinks a week and takes no supplements or over the counter iron. His brother was recently found to carry the same genetic result. On examination his liver edge is palpable 2 cm below the costal margin and is smooth and non-tender, with no splenomegaly, no spider naevi and no ascites. His ferritin is 1250 micrograms/L (30 to 300), transferrin saturation is 68 per cent (16 to 45), alanine aminotransferase is 74 U/L (less than 40) and platelets are 224 x10^9/L (150 to 400). Genetic testing reports homozygosity for the C282Y variant of the HFE gene. His fasting glucose and HbA1c are within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Smooth non-tender liver edge palpable 2 cm below the costal margin, no splenomegaly, no spider naevi, no palmar erythema, no ascites, mild tenderness over both second and third metacarpophalangeal joints without synovitis, skin of normal colour
data_table.Investigations: Ferritin 1250 micrograms/L (30 to 300), transferrin saturation 68 per cent (16 to 45), alanine aminotransferase 74 U/L (less than 40), gamma glutamyl transferase 62 U/L (less than 60), bilirubin and albumin within normal limits, platelets 224 x10^9/L (150 to 400), international normalised ratio 1.0, HFE genotype homozygous C282Y, fasting glucose and HbA1c within normal limits, hepatitis B and C serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Start oral deferasirox and monitor his ferritin every three months
options.rationale: Oral iron chelation is reserved for iron overload where venesection is not possible, principally transfusion dependent anaemias, because it is expensive and carries renal, hepatic and gastrointestinal toxicity. A man who can donate blood safely should be venesected instead. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Haemochromatosis clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Haemochromatosis clinical update

options.text: Advise a low iron diet with avoidance of red meat and vitamin C
options.rationale: Dietary modification has a negligible effect on total body iron stores compared with venesection and imposes a restrictive diet for little return. Sensible advice is limited to avoiding iron and high dose vitamin C supplements, uncooked shellfish and excess alcohol. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Haemochromatosis clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Haemochromatosis clinical update

options.text: Begin weekly venesection and assess him for liver fibrosis
options.rationale: Homozygosity for C282Y with a ferritin well above 1000 micrograms/L, a high transferrin saturation and raised transaminases establishes clinically expressed iron overload, and weekly venesection of 450 to 500 mL is started to deplete iron stores while fibrosis is assessed, because a ferritin above 1000 micrograms/L with raised transaminases and low platelets is the recognised trigger for evaluating advanced fibrosis. Transient elastography with or without liver biopsy is used for that assessment, and identifying cirrhosis mandates hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance that iron depletion alone does not remove. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Haemochromatosis clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Haemochromatosis clinical update

options.text: Repeat the iron studies in six months before committing to treatment
options.rationale: Deferring treatment at this level of iron loading allows ongoing deposition in liver, heart, pancreas and joints, and the diagnosis is not in doubt with a concordant genotype and biochemistry. Repeat testing is the right approach to a mildly raised ferritin with a normal transferrin saturation, where inflammation or alcohol is the likelier explanation. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Haemochromatosis clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Haemochromatosis clinical update

options.text: Refer for magnetic resonance imaging to quantify cardiac iron loading
options.rationale: Cardiac iron quantification is important in transfusional overload such as thalassaemia, where myocardial loading dominates the prognosis, but clinically significant cardiac involvement is uncommon in this condition and is not part of routine initial assessment. Cardiac imaging is added if there are symptoms or signs of cardiac dysfunction. (Source: HSANZ: Iron overload guidance)

explanation.summary: Hereditary haemochromatosis from HFE C282Y homozygosity is one of the commonest genetic conditions in Australians of northern European ancestry, with a carrier frequency that makes homozygosity present in roughly 1 in 200 people, although penetrance is incomplete and many homozygotes never develop iron overload. The diagnostic sequence runs from transferrin saturation and ferritin through to genotyping, and it is the biochemistry rather than the genotype that determines whether treatment is needed. Venesection is remarkably effective, with weekly removal of 450 to 500 mL of blood shedding around 200 to 250 mg of iron each time, continued until the ferritin falls to the low normal range and then spaced as maintenance for life. Crucially, iron depletion reverses fatigue, reduces transaminases and improves skin pigmentation and glycaemic control, but it does not reverse established cirrhosis or arthropathy, which is why fibrosis assessment matters at diagnosis and why anyone found to be cirrhotic enters six monthly hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance regardless of how well their ferritin is subsequently controlled. First degree relatives are offered screening with iron studies and genotyping.
key_points: Biochemistry, not genotype, determines the need for treatment
Ferritin above 1000 micrograms/L with raised transaminases triggers fibrosis assessment
Weekly venesection removes around 200 to 250 mg of iron per session
Iron depletion does not reverse established cirrhosis or arthropathy
First degree relatives are offered iron studies and genotyping
explanation.pearls: Cirrhosis established before treatment carries an ongoing hepatocellular carcinoma risk of roughly 3 to 4 per cent per year that venesection does not abolish, so six monthly ultrasound surveillance continues indefinitely even once the ferritin has been normal for years.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Haemochromatosis clinical update

subtopic_detail: An alkaline phosphatase of 620 with normal liver enzymes and bone pain over one shin in a man whose hearing has declined
stem:
You are the general physician seeing a 71 year old man referred because of a persistently raised alkaline phosphatase found on routine testing, together with eighteen months of a deep ache over his right shin that is worse at night.

He has also noticed his hearing has declined over two years and his hat feels tighter than it used to. On examination the right tibia is warm to touch with a palpable anterior bow, and there is tenderness on percussion over it. Weber testing lateralises to the right and Rinne is negative on the right. His alkaline phosphatase is 620 U/L (30 to 110) with gamma glutamyl transferase, alanine aminotransferase and bilirubin all within normal limits. His corrected calcium is 2.38 mmol/L (2.20 to 2.60), phosphate is within normal limits, 25 hydroxyvitamin D is 68 nmol/L (greater than 50) and his estimated glomerular filtration rate is above 60 mL/min/1.73m2. Plain radiographs of the right tibia show coarsened trabeculae with cortical thickening and a flame shaped lytic front.

data_table.Examination: Right tibia warm to touch with an anterior bow and tenderness on percussion, increased skull circumference reported by the patient, Weber lateralises to the right with a negative right Rinne test, no spinal tenderness, no focal neurological deficit in the lower limbs
data_table.Investigations: Alkaline phosphatase 620 U/L (30 to 110) with gamma glutamyl transferase, alanine aminotransferase and bilirubin within normal limits, corrected calcium 2.38 mmol/L (2.20 to 2.60), phosphate within normal limits, 25 hydroxyvitamin D 68 nmol/L (greater than 50), parathyroid hormone within normal limits, estimated glomerular filtration rate above 60 mL/min/1.73m2, radiographs of the right tibia showing coarsened trabeculae, cortical thickening and a flame shaped lytic front

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Refer for bone biopsy of the tibial lesion before starting any treatment
options.rationale: The radiographic and biochemical picture is characteristic enough that biopsy is not required, and it carries a risk of fracture through abnormal bone. Biopsy is reserved for atypical imaging or for suspicion of sarcomatous transformation, which presents with a rapid rise in pain, a soft tissue mass or cortical destruction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Arrange serum electrophoresis and skeletal survey for myeloma
options.rationale: Myeloma characteristically produces punched out lytic lesions with a normal or only mildly raised alkaline phosphatase, because osteoblastic activity is suppressed rather than increased. The markedly raised alkaline phosphatase with cortical thickening points away from it. (Source: HSANZ: Myeloma diagnosis and management)

options.text: Replace vitamin D and recheck his alkaline phosphatase in three months
options.rationale: His 25 hydroxyvitamin D is already adequate at 68 nmol/L with a normal calcium, phosphate and parathyroid hormone, so there is no deficiency to correct. Osteomalacia produces a low or low normal calcium and phosphate with secondary hyperparathyroidism, a pattern absent here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start denosumab six monthly and arrange bone density measurement
options.rationale: Denosumab treats osteoporosis, a disease of reduced bone quantity, whereas the radiographic picture here is of disordered and excessive bone turnover with cortical thickening. Bone density measurement in an affected bone is also misleading because the abnormal bone reads as dense. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give a single intravenous zoledronic acid infusion after dental review
options.rationale: Focal bone pain with a warm bowed tibia, radiographic coarsened trabeculae with a flame shaped lytic front, and a markedly raised alkaline phosphatase with normal liver enzymes identify Paget disease of bone, and a single 5 mg zoledronic acid infusion is the treatment of choice because it produces prolonged biochemical remission in the great majority. Dental assessment precedes any potent bisphosphonate, and calcium and vitamin D are ensured beforehand to prevent post-infusion hypocalcaemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Paget disease of bone is a focal disorder of accelerated and disorganised bone remodelling that affects around 1 to 2 per cent of Australians over 55, and it is most often discovered incidentally through an isolated rise in alkaline phosphatase or an abnormal radiograph. The pelvis, spine, skull, femur and tibia are the sites most involved, and the clinical consequences follow the anatomy: bone pain, bowing deformity with secondary osteoarthritis in adjacent joints, pathological fracture, skull enlargement with conductive or sensorineural hearing loss from involvement of the temporal bone and auditory ossicles, and occasionally high output cardiac failure or cranial nerve compression. An isolated raised alkaline phosphatase with normal gamma glutamyl transferase and liver enzymes localises the origin to bone rather than the biliary tree, and a nuclear medicine bone scan is the usual means of mapping the full extent of disease once the diagnosis is suspected. Treatment with a potent bisphosphonate is indicated for symptomatic disease and for asymptomatic disease at sites where complications would be serious, such as the skull base or a weight bearing long bone, and a single zoledronic acid infusion normalises alkaline phosphatase in around 90 per cent with remission lasting years.
key_points: An isolated raised alkaline phosphatase with normal liver enzymes localises to bone
Coarsened trabeculae with cortical thickening distinguishes it from lytic myeloma
Hearing loss reflects temporal bone and ossicular involvement
A single zoledronic acid infusion achieves prolonged remission in most patients
Ensure vitamin D repletion and dental review before a potent bisphosphonate
explanation.pearls: Sarcomatous transformation occurs in well under 1 per cent but is nearly always fatal, and the warning sign is a change in the character of pain from a chronic ache to severe unremitting pain with a soft tissue mass, which warrants urgent imaging rather than an increase in analgesia.

subtopic_detail: An alkaline phosphatase still twice the upper limit after fourteen months of weight based ursodeoxycholic acid taken reliably, with a normal bilirubin
stem:
You are the gastroenterology registrar reviewing a 54 year old woman whose primary biliary cholangitis was diagnosed fourteen months ago on a cholestatic liver profile with a positive antimitochondrial antibody. She was started on ursodeoxycholic acid at 14 mg/kg daily and a pharmacy dispensing record confirms she has collected every script.

She remains troubled by fatigue and by itch that wakes her at night. On examination she has excoriations over both forearms and mild xanthelasma, with no jaundice, ascites or asterixis and a liver edge that is not palpable. Her alkaline phosphatase is 248 U/L (30 to 110), having fallen from 410 U/L at diagnosis, while her bilirubin is 12 micromol/L (less than 20) and albumin is 39 g/L (35 to 50). Her alanine aminotransferase is 52 U/L (less than 40), anti smooth muscle antibody is negative and immunoglobulin G is within normal limits. Transient elastography measures 7.1 kPa and her platelets are 226 x10^9/L (150 to 400).

data_table.Examination: Excoriations over both forearms, mild xanthelasma, no jaundice, no ascites, no asterixis, liver edge not palpable, no splenomegaly, body mass index 26 kg/m2
data_table.Investigations: Alkaline phosphatase 248 U/L (30 to 110), down from 410 U/L at diagnosis; gamma glutamyl transferase 186 U/L (less than 60); alanine aminotransferase 52 U/L (less than 40); bilirubin 12 micromol/L (less than 20); albumin 39 g/L (35 to 50); international normalised ratio 1.0; platelets 226 x10^9/L (150 to 400); antimitochondrial antibody positive; anti smooth muscle antibody negative; immunoglobulin G within normal limits; transient elastography 7.1 kPa; abdominal ultrasound showing no biliary dilatation and a normal spleen

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Add a second line agent and continue the ursodeoxycholic acid
options.rationale: An alkaline phosphatase persisting above roughly 1.5 to 1.67 times the upper limit of normal after twelve months of weight based ursodeoxycholic acid defines an inadequate biochemical response, which identifies the third or so of patients whose long term risk of progression remains raised and who benefit from a second agent such as obeticholic acid or a fibrate added to the existing treatment. The ursodeoxycholic acid is continued rather than substituted, because the second agent is additive and its trial evidence was generated on a background of established therapy. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Primary biliary cholangitis clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Primary biliary cholangitis clinical update

options.text: Increase her ursodeoxycholic acid dose above 20 mg/kg daily
options.rationale: Doses beyond the 13 to 15 mg/kg range confer no additional biochemical or survival benefit and increase diarrhoea, so escalation within the same drug does not rescue an inadequate response. Checking that the dose is genuinely within the weight based range is worthwhile, and hers already is. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Primary biliary cholangitis clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Primary biliary cholangitis clinical update

options.text: Start prednisolone with azathioprine as for autoimmune hepatitis
options.rationale: Immunosuppression is the treatment for an autoimmune hepatitis overlap, which requires a markedly raised alanine aminotransferase with a raised immunoglobulin G or positive smooth muscle antibody and interface hepatitis on biopsy. Her transaminase is only mildly raised with negative smooth muscle antibody and a normal immunoglobulin G, which argues against overlap. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Refer for magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography urgently
options.rationale: Cholangiography is used where a large duct obstruction or primary sclerosing cholangitis is suspected, and her antimitochondrial antibody positivity with a normal ultrasound and no biliary dilatation makes a structural lesion unlikely. Imaging would be indicated if her bilirubin rose or cholestasis worsened abruptly. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Primary biliary cholangitis clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Primary biliary cholangitis clinical update

options.text: Continue her current treatment and repeat the liver tests yearly
options.rationale: Annual monitoring without change is appropriate for a patient who has achieved an adequate biochemical response, since their survival approaches that of the general population. Accepting an alkaline phosphatase at this level leaves a treatable excess risk of cirrhosis and transplantation unaddressed. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Primary biliary cholangitis clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Primary biliary cholangitis clinical update

explanation.summary: Primary biliary cholangitis is a chronic autoimmune cholangiopathy that destroys small intrahepatic bile ducts, affects women roughly nine times more often than men, and is diagnosed without biopsy when a cholestatic liver profile is accompanied by a positive antimitochondrial antibody. Ursodeoxycholic acid at 13 to 15 mg/kg daily is first line for everyone and transforms prognosis in those who respond, but between a quarter and a third of patients have an inadequate biochemical response, and the alkaline phosphatase at twelve months is the practical marker that separates the two groups because it predicts progression to cirrhosis, transplantation and death. Recognising inadequate response matters because effective second line agents now exist and are added to rather than substituted for the original drug. Alongside disease modifying treatment, management addresses the symptom burden and the complications that are easy to overlook, namely pruritus treated first with a bile acid sequestrant, fatigue, bone density surveillance for the osteoporosis that accompanies chronic cholestasis, fat soluble vitamin status, and six monthly hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance once cirrhosis is present.
key_points: Cholestatic enzymes with a positive antimitochondrial antibody diagnose it without biopsy
Ursodeoxycholic acid 13 to 15 mg/kg daily is first line for all patients
Alkaline phosphatase at twelve months separates adequate from inadequate responders
A second line agent is added to, not substituted for, ursodeoxycholic acid
Manage pruritus, bone density and fat soluble vitamins alongside disease modification
explanation.pearls: A bile acid sequestrant for pruritus binds ursodeoxycholic acid in the gut as well as bile salts, so cholestyramine must be separated from the ursodeoxycholic acid dose by at least four hours or the apparent treatment failure is simply a drug interaction.

subtopic_detail: A positive breath test six weeks after completing a week of amoxicillin, clarithromycin and a proton pump inhibitor for a duodenal ulcer
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 52 year old woman who had a duodenal ulcer found on gastroscopy three months ago with a positive gastric biopsy for Helicobacter pylori. She completed seven days of esomeprazole, amoxicillin and clarithromycin and reports she took every dose.

Her epigastric pain improved but has returned over the past fortnight. She stopped her proton pump inhibitor two weeks before testing and has taken no antibiotics since the eradication course. A urea breath test performed six weeks after finishing treatment is positive. Her appetite, weight and swallowing are unchanged and her haemoglobin and ferritin are within normal limits. She tolerates penicillins and has previously taken clarithromycin twice for chest infections.

data_table.Examination: Mild epigastric tenderness without guarding, no mass, no hepatosplenomegaly, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Urea breath test positive six weeks after completing eradication therapy with the proton pump inhibitor withheld for two weeks beforehand, haemoglobin within normal limits, ferritin within normal limits, gastroscopy three months ago showing a 10 mm duodenal ulcer with biopsy positive for Helicobacter pylori and no malignancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Refer for repeat gastroscopy with biopsy for antibiotic susceptibility testing
options.rationale: Culture directed therapy is a legitimate approach but is generally reserved for patients who have failed two or more courses, since it requires endoscopy and specialised culture that is not universally available. Her ulcer was benign on biopsy three months ago and she has no alarm features requiring repeat endoscopy now. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Repeat the identical seven day regimen for a further fourteen days
options.rationale: Reusing clarithromycin after a failed clarithromycin containing course is the principal error in this situation, because failure usually reflects acquired or pre-existing macrolide resistance that a longer duration will not overcome. Prior macrolide exposure for respiratory infection makes resistance still more likely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Prescribe second line therapy that avoids the antibiotic already used
options.rationale: Second line treatment after a failed clarithromycin based regimen substitutes agents to which resistance is unlikely, using a proton pump inhibitor with amoxicillin plus either metronidazole and bismuth or a quinolone such as levofloxacin, and confirmation of eradication is arranged again afterwards. Avoiding repeat exposure to the failed antibiotic is the governing principle of salvage therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Continue long term proton pump inhibitor therapy without further antibiotics
options.rationale: Acid suppression heals ulcers but leaves the organism in place, so ulcer recurrence and the long term risks of gastric cancer and lymphoma persist. Indefinite acid suppression alone is a strategy for reflux disease, not for an untreated infection with a documented duodenal ulcer. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Repeat the breath test in three months before any further treatment
options.rationale: The test was performed correctly six weeks after therapy with the proton pump inhibitor appropriately withheld, so the positive result is reliable and repeating it simply delays treatment. A repeat would be justified if acid suppression or antibiotics had been taken shortly beforehand, since both cause false negatives rather than false positives. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

explanation.summary: Helicobacter pylori eradication cures peptic ulcer disease and reduces the risk of gastric adenocarcinoma and mucosa associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma, so confirming success matters and is recommended for all treated patients, particularly those with an ulcer. Australian first line therapy pairs a proton pump inhibitor with amoxicillin and clarithromycin for seven days, and reported eradication rates have fallen as clarithromycin resistance has risen. Testing for cure requires the proton pump inhibitor to be stopped for at least two weeks and antibiotics for four, and the test performed at least four weeks after finishing treatment, because acid suppression and recent antibiotics suppress the organism and generate false negatives. When treatment fails, the governing principle of salvage therapy is not to reuse an antibiotic to which resistance has probably been selected, so clarithromycin is dropped and replaced by a bismuth based quadruple regimen or a levofloxacin containing combination, with amoxicillin usually retained because resistance to it remains uncommon. Repeated failure is the point at which endoscopy with culture and susceptibility testing earns its place.
key_points: Confirm eradication in all treated patients, especially those with an ulcer
Withhold the proton pump inhibitor two weeks and antibiotics four weeks before testing
Failure usually reflects clarithromycin resistance, which repeat exposure will not overcome
Salvage regimens substitute bismuth and metronidazole or a quinolone
Culture directed therapy follows two or more failures
explanation.pearls: Amoxicillin resistance in Helicobacter pylori remains under about 5 per cent in Australia while clarithromycin resistance has climbed well above 15 per cent, which is why amoxicillin is carried forward into the second line regimen while clarithromycin is abandoned.

subtopic_detail: Grittiness in both eyes and a mouth so dry she carries water to swallow bread, with bilateral parotid swelling and a positive anti-Ro
stem:
You are the general physician seeing a 53 year old woman with two years of gritty eyes that feel as though sand is in them by late afternoon, and a mouth so dry that she keeps a water bottle beside her and cannot swallow bread without a drink.

She has had three episodes of painless swelling in front of both ears over the past year, and has developed six new dental caries in eighteen months after decades without any. She takes no anticholinergic medication, no antihistamine and no diuretic. On examination both parotid glands are mildly enlarged and non-tender, her tongue is dry and fissured with loss of the normal salivary pooling, and there is no joint swelling or rash. Her antinuclear antibody is positive at a titre of 1 in 640 with a positive anti-Ro antibody, rheumatoid factor is positive at low titre and her anti-double stranded DNA is negative.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral mild non-tender parotid enlargement, dry fissured tongue with absent salivary pooling in the floor of the mouth, multiple dental restorations and caries, no synovitis, no malar or discoid rash, no Raynaud phenomenon, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Antinuclear antibody positive at 1 in 640, anti-Ro antibody positive, anti-La antibody positive, rheumatoid factor positive at low titre, anti-double stranded DNA negative, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 34 mm/h (less than 20), full blood count within normal limits, urea electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits, protein electrophoresis showing a polyclonal increase in immunoglobulins

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Start hydroxychloroquine and arrange ophthalmology baseline screening
options.rationale: Hydroxychloroquine is used for the arthralgia and fatigue of this condition but has not been shown to improve dryness, which is her dominant problem, and it is not the initial step. Its introduction is reasonable later if inflammatory arthralgia or fatigue persist. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Start prednisolone 25 mg daily and taper over the next three months
options.rationale: Systemic corticosteroids do not restore glandular function in established disease and carry substantial harm over months of use. They are reserved for significant extraglandular manifestations such as interstitial lung disease, vasculitis or renal involvement. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Refer for parotid biopsy to establish the diagnosis before any treatment
options.rationale: Labial gland biopsy is used when the antibody profile is negative and the diagnosis remains uncertain, and here a positive anti-Ro with characteristic sicca symptoms and objective dryness makes it unnecessary. Biopsy also becomes important if a persistent unilateral parotid mass raises the possibility of lymphoma. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Sjogren syndrome information)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Sjogren syndrome information

options.text: Trial pilocarpine with intensive dental and ocular surface care
options.rationale: A muscarinic agonist is a reasonable step for residual glandular function and intensive local care is essential, but committing to pharmacological stimulation before the dryness has been objectively quantified and organ involvement assessed puts treatment ahead of assessment. The local care component of this answer is correct while its sequencing is not. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Sjogren syndrome information)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Sjogren syndrome information

options.text: Quantify dryness objectively and screen for systemic organ involvement
options.rationale: Sicca symptoms with parotid swelling, accelerated caries and a positive anti-Ro establish the clinical diagnosis, and the next step is objective measurement with Schirmer testing and ocular surface staining plus salivary flow assessment, alongside screening for extraglandular disease with renal function, urinalysis for renal tubular acidosis, thyroid function, immunoglobulins and cryoglobulins, and baseline chest imaging. This assessment defines both the severity of dryness and the presence of systemic involvement that determines whether treatment goes beyond local measures. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Sjogren syndrome information)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Sjogren syndrome information

explanation.summary: Sjogren syndrome is a chronic autoimmune exocrinopathy that predominantly affects women in middle age and causes lymphocytic infiltration of lacrimal and salivary glands, producing dry eyes and dry mouth with their downstream complications of corneal damage, accelerated dental caries, oral candidiasis and difficulty with speech and swallowing. It is far more than a nuisance disease, because extraglandular involvement includes interstitial lung disease, renal tubular acidosis and interstitial nephritis, peripheral neuropathy, cutaneous and systemic vasculitis, and profound fatigue, and because it carries a markedly increased risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Diagnosis rests on objective evidence of dryness alongside either a positive anti-Ro antibody or a labial gland biopsy showing focal lymphocytic sialadenitis, and the important mimics are anticholinergic and other drug effects, previous head and neck radiotherapy, sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, hepatitis C and immunoglobulin G4 related disease. Management is largely local and preventive, with tear substitutes, punctal occlusion, saliva substitutes and rigorous dental care, adding muscarinic agonists for residual glandular function and reserving immunosuppression for extraglandular disease.
key_points: Objective dryness plus anti-Ro positivity or a labial biopsy establishes the diagnosis
Accelerated dental caries and parotid swelling are characteristic features
Extraglandular disease includes lung, renal tubular, neurological and vasculitic involvement
Management is mainly local; immunosuppression is for systemic involvement
Drugs, prior radiotherapy, sarcoidosis and hepatitis C are the mimics to exclude
explanation.pearls: Lymphoma risk is roughly 5 to 15 times that of the general population and the clinical warning sign is a persistently enlarged unilateral parotid gland, so asymmetric or progressive glandular swelling prompts imaging and biopsy rather than reassurance, and a falling immunoglobulin M or the appearance of a monoclonal band is a laboratory signal of the same concern.

subtopic_detail: Difficulty rising from a chair with a violaceous rash over the knuckles and upper back in a woman whose creatine kinase is 1800
stem:
You are the general physician seeing a 61 year old woman with ten weeks of progressive difficulty rising from a chair and lifting her arms to wash her hair. She has also noticed a rash.

She has lost 4 kg without trying and has mild difficulty swallowing solids. On examination there are violaceous scaly papules over the extensor surfaces of both second and third metacarpophalangeal joints, a confluent violaceous erythema across her upper back and shoulders, and periorbital violaceous discolouration. Shoulder abduction and hip flexion are graded 3 out of 5 bilaterally with normal distal power and normal reflexes. Her creatine kinase is 1800 U/L (less than 200), alanine aminotransferase is 88 U/L (less than 40), and antinuclear antibody is positive with a positive anti-Mi-2 antibody. Electromyography shows a myopathic pattern with spontaneous activity and her magnetic resonance imaging of the thighs shows patchy muscle oedema.

data_table.Examination: Violaceous scaly papules over the extensor aspects of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints, confluent violaceous erythema across the upper back and shoulders, periorbital violaceous discolouration, shoulder abduction and hip flexion 3 out of 5 bilaterally with normal distal power, reflexes normal and symmetrical, no synovitis, no sclerodactyly, chest clear on auscultation
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 1800 U/L (less than 200), alanine aminotransferase 88 U/L (less than 40), lactate dehydrogenase raised, antinuclear antibody positive with anti-Mi-2 antibody positive, anti-Jo-1 negative, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, electromyography showing a myopathic pattern with spontaneous activity, magnetic resonance imaging of the thighs showing patchy muscle oedema, chest radiograph reported as normal

lead_in: What is the most important next step alongside starting corticosteroid treatment?

options.text: Age appropriate malignancy screening including computed tomography imaging
options.rationale: Dermatomyositis in an adult of this age carries a substantially increased risk of underlying malignancy, concentrated in the three years either side of diagnosis, so a structured search is undertaken at diagnosis with computed tomography of chest, abdomen and pelvis, mammography, cervical screening and gastrointestinal investigation guided by symptoms. Identifying an occult cancer changes both the prognosis and the treatment, because the myositis often improves when the tumour is treated. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Inflammatory myopathies information)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Inflammatory myopathies information

options.text: Muscle biopsy of the most severely affected proximal muscle group
options.rationale: Biopsy remains useful where the diagnosis is uncertain, but the combination of pathognomonic skin findings, proximal weakness, a raised creatine kinase, a myositis specific antibody and characteristic imaging makes this diagnosis secure without it. Sampling the most severely affected muscle also risks a non-diagnostic end stage specimen. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Inflammatory myopathies information)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Inflammatory myopathies information

options.text: Nerve conduction studies to exclude a coexisting peripheral neuropathy
options.rationale: Her weakness is proximal and symmetrical with preserved distal power and normal reflexes, which is a myopathic rather than a neuropathic pattern, and electromyography has already demonstrated a myopathic process. Nerve conduction studies would be indicated for distal weakness with sensory loss or absent reflexes. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Inflammatory myopathies information)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Inflammatory myopathies information

options.text: Referral for immediate plasma exchange and intravenous immunoglobulin
options.rationale: Intravenous immunoglobulin has an established role in refractory disease or where there is severe dysphagia or respiratory muscle involvement, but it is not first line and plasma exchange has not been shown to help in inflammatory myopathy. Corticosteroids with a steroid sparing agent are the initial treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Ambulatory electrocardiographic monitoring for myocarditis over 24 hours
options.rationale: Cardiac involvement does occur and warrants assessment with electrocardiography, troponin and echocardiography, but prolonged rhythm monitoring is not the priority in the absence of symptoms, and it does not address the malignancy question that dominates prognosis. Rhythm monitoring becomes relevant with documented cardiac involvement or arrhythmic symptoms. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

explanation.summary: Dermatomyositis combines a symmetrical proximal inflammatory myopathy with characteristic cutaneous features, of which Gottron papules over the knuckles and the shawl and heliotrope distributions of violaceous erythema are the most specific. Diagnosis rests on the clinical pattern supported by a raised creatine kinase, myositis specific antibodies, electromyography and magnetic resonance imaging, with biopsy reserved for uncertainty. The two assessments that must accompany diagnosis in an adult are a search for occult malignancy and evaluation of the organs that determine mortality: interstitial lung disease, which is particularly associated with anti-melanoma differentiation associated gene 5 and antisynthetase antibodies and can be rapidly progressive, oesophageal and pharyngeal involvement causing aspiration, and cardiac involvement. The malignancy association is strongest in adults over 45, is concentrated within three years either side of the myositis diagnosis, and in Australian practice the commonest associated tumours are ovarian, lung, breast, gastrointestinal and haematological, with nasopharyngeal carcinoma prominent in patients of South East Asian ancestry. Treatment starts with high dose corticosteroid and an early steroid sparing agent such as methotrexate or azathioprine, with intravenous immunoglobulin for severe or refractory disease.
key_points: Gottron papules and heliotrope and shawl erythema are the specific cutaneous signs
Malignancy risk is concentrated within three years either side of diagnosis
Screen for interstitial lung disease, dysphagia and cardiac involvement at diagnosis
Proximal symmetrical weakness with normal reflexes is a myopathic pattern
Corticosteroid with an early steroid sparing agent is the initial treatment
explanation.pearls: Antibody profile predicts the complication to fear: anti-Mi-2 associates with classic skin disease and a good treatment response, anti-melanoma differentiation associated gene 5 with rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease and often a normal creatine kinase, and anti-transcription intermediary factor 1 gamma with the highest malignancy risk of all, in the order of a third to a half of patients.

subtopic_detail: Visible blood in the urine appearing on the second day of a sore throat in a young man with protein of 1.2 grams per day and normal complement
stem:
You are the nephrology registrar seeing a 24 year old man referred after three episodes of visibly bloody urine over two years. He describes the urine as being the colour of cola, and on each occasion it began on the second day of a sore throat and cleared within four days.

He is well between episodes with no oedema, no rash and no joint pain. His blood pressure today is 142/88 mmHg on two readings. Urine microscopy shows dysmorphic red cells with red cell casts. His protein excretion is 1.2 g per day, creatinine is 96 micromol/L with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 88 mL/min/1.73m2, and his albumin is within normal limits. Complement C3 and C4 are both within normal limits, antinuclear antibody and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies are negative, hepatitis B and C serology are negative, and his antistreptolysin O titre is not raised. Renal ultrasound shows two normal sized kidneys with no structural abnormality.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72 beats per minute, blood pressure 142/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: No peripheral or periorbital oedema, no rash or purpura, no synovitis, no lymphadenopathy, chest clear, abdomen soft with no renal angle tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Urine microscopy with dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts, urinary protein 1.2 g per day, creatinine 96 micromol/L with estimated glomerular filtration rate 88 mL/min/1.73m2, albumin within normal limits, complement C3 and C4 within normal limits, antinuclear antibody negative, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies negative, hepatitis B and C serology negative, antistreptolysin O titre not raised, renal ultrasound showing two normal sized kidneys

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Start high dose prednisolone and cyclophosphamide without delay
options.rationale: Aggressive immunosuppression is the treatment for rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with crescents and falling renal function, and his function is preserved with a two year history of intermittent episodes. Commencing cyclophosphamide before histology risks substantial toxicity including infertility and malignancy for a disease that may not require it. (Source: KHA-CARI: Management of glomerulonephritis)

options.text: Arrange cystoscopy and computed tomography urography to exclude a tumour
options.rationale: Urological imaging and cystoscopy are the pathway for non-glomerular bleeding, and dysmorphic red cells with red cell casts and proteinuria localise the bleeding to the glomerulus. Urothelial malignancy would also be very unlikely at 24 with no smoking history or risk factors. (Source: KHA-CARI: Management of glomerulonephritis)

options.text: Start renin angiotensin blockade and refer for renal biopsy
options.rationale: Recurrent visible haematuria synchronous with upper respiratory infection, glomerular red cells with casts, proteinuria above 1 g per day, hypertension and normal complement is the classic presentation of immunoglobulin A nephropathy, and biopsy is indicated because proteinuria at this level with hypertension identifies a patient at risk of progression whose histological features guide immunosuppression. Renin angiotensin blockade is started immediately with a blood pressure and proteinuria target, since it is the intervention that most reduces long term progression. (Source: KHA-CARI: Management of glomerulonephritis)

options.text: Give a course of penicillin and repeat his urinalysis in six weeks
options.rationale: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis follows a pharyngitis by one to three weeks with a low C3 and a raised antistreptolysin O titre, whereas his haematuria begins within a day or two of the sore throat with normal complement and no serological evidence of streptococcal infection. That latency difference is the classic discriminator between the two conditions. (Source: KHA-CARI: Management of glomerulonephritis)

options.text: Reassure him and arrange annual urinalysis and blood pressure checks
options.rationale: Annual surveillance is appropriate for isolated microscopic haematuria with normal blood pressure, no proteinuria and normal renal function, and he fails all three of those conditions. Proteinuria above 1 g per day with hypertension marks him as being at genuine risk of progressive loss of function. (Source: KHA-CARI: Management of glomerulonephritis)

explanation.summary: Immunoglobulin A nephropathy is the commonest primary glomerulonephritis worldwide and typically presents in young adults either with recurrent visible haematuria coinciding with mucosal infection or, more insidiously, with microscopic haematuria and proteinuria found incidentally. The characteristic timing of synpharyngitic haematuria, beginning within a day or two of an upper respiratory infection, distinguishes it from post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, which follows a latent period of one to three weeks and is accompanied by a depressed C3 and serological evidence of recent streptococcal infection. The initial task with any haematuria is to establish whether it is glomerular, and dysmorphic red cells, red cell casts and proteinuria settle that question and redirect the patient away from urological investigation. Prognosis is far from uniformly benign, with a substantial minority progressing to end stage kidney disease over decades, and the adverse markers are proteinuria above 1 g per day, hypertension, reduced function at presentation and specific histological features. Management centres on optimised supportive care with renin angiotensin blockade titrated to reduce proteinuria, blood pressure control, sodium restriction and sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibition, with immunosuppression reserved for those at high risk of progression despite this.
key_points: Haematuria within a day or two of pharyngitis suggests immunoglobulin A nephropathy
Post-streptococcal disease has a one to three week latency and a low C3
Dysmorphic red cells with casts localise bleeding to the glomerulus
Proteinuria above 1 g per day with hypertension predicts progression
Renin angiotensin blockade titrated to proteinuria is the mainstay of treatment
explanation.pearls: Proteinuria is both the strongest prognostic marker and the treatment target, and reducing it below 1 g per day, ideally towards 0.5 g, is associated with markedly better long term outcomes, which is why the dose of renin angiotensin blockade is titrated to the proteinuria rather than to blood pressure alone.

subtopic_detail: Eight loose motions a day with abdominal cramping six weeks into pembrolizumab for melanoma, with negative stool cultures
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 64 year old man in the oncology day unit who has had six weeks of pembrolizumab for metastatic melanoma. Over the past five days he has developed increasingly frequent loose motions, now eight a day including two overnight, with cramping lower abdominal pain.

He reports a small amount of blood mixed through the stool yesterday. He has not travelled, has taken no antibiotics and no one else at home is unwell. His vital signs are pulse 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in air and temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius. His abdomen is soft with generalised tenderness but no guarding or rebound, and bowel sounds are present. Stool cultures and Clostridioides difficile toxin testing are negative, his C reactive protein is 68 mg/L (less than 5), and computed tomography of the abdomen shows diffuse colonic wall thickening with mucosal hyperenhancement and no perforation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with generalised tenderness, no guarding or rebound, bowel sounds present, mucous membranes slightly dry, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Stool culture negative, Clostridioides difficile toxin negative, stool viral panel negative, C reactive protein 68 mg/L (less than 5), albumin 32 g/L (35 to 50), potassium 3.3 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), creatinine 94 micromol/L, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, morning cortisol within normal limits, computed tomography of the abdomen showing diffuse colonic wall thickening with mucosal hyperenhancement and no perforation or free gas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Start oral vancomycin empirically and repeat the toxin assay in 48 hours
options.rationale: Empirical treatment for Clostridioides difficile is not justified when the toxin assay is negative, he has had no antibiotic exposure, and a non-infective cause is strongly supported by the timing and imaging. Repeat testing would delay effective treatment of the actual pathology. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Refer for urgent colonoscopy with biopsies before any treatment is started
options.rationale: Endoscopy is useful to confirm the diagnosis and assess severity and can be performed once treatment is under way, but it carries perforation risk in an inflamed colon and should not delay corticosteroid therapy in a patient with grade 3 disease. Flexible sigmoidoscopy is most valuable where the diagnosis is genuinely uncertain or the response to steroids is poor. (Source: eviQ: Immune related adverse events management)
source_refs: eviQ: Immune related adverse events management

options.text: Replace potassium, give intravenous fluids and reassess him in 24 hours
options.rationale: Correcting hypokalaemia and volume depletion is necessary supportive care but as the sole plan it leaves the immune mediated inflammation untreated for a further day during which perforation can occur. Supportive measures accompany rather than substitute for immunosuppression. (Source: eviQ: Immune related adverse events management)
source_refs: eviQ: Immune related adverse events management

options.text: Give loperamide regularly and continue his immunotherapy as scheduled
options.rationale: Antimotility agents mask the severity of immune mediated colitis and delay recognition of a condition that can progress to perforation, so they are avoided once colitis is suspected. Loperamide is appropriate for mild grade 1 diarrhoea without abdominal pain, blood or raised inflammatory markers. (Source: eviQ: Immune related adverse events management)
source_refs: eviQ: Immune related adverse events management

options.text: Withhold the immunotherapy and start high dose corticosteroid treatment
options.rationale: Eight stools a day with abdominal pain, blood and radiological colitis on a checkpoint inhibitor, with infection excluded, is grade 3 immune mediated colitis requiring the drug to be withheld and corticosteroid started at 1 to 2 mg/kg of prednisolone equivalent, usually intravenously with admission at this severity. Infliximab or vedolizumab is added if there is no response within about three days, and a rapid steroid taper over at least four to six weeks follows improvement. (Source: eviQ: Immune related adverse events management)
source_refs: eviQ: Immune related adverse events management

explanation.summary: Immune checkpoint inhibitors have transformed the treatment of melanoma, lung and renal cancers and other tumours, and their characteristic toxicities arise from loss of immune tolerance rather than from cytotoxicity, so they behave like autoimmune disease and respond to immunosuppression. Colitis is among the commonest and most dangerous, more frequent with cytotoxic T lymphocyte antigen 4 blockade such as ipilimumab than with programmed cell death protein 1 blockade, and more frequent again with combination therapy, and it can occur weeks to many months after treatment starts or even after it has stopped. Severity is graded by stool frequency above baseline together with abdominal pain, blood and systemic features, and management is graded in parallel: supportive measures for mild disease, oral corticosteroid with drug interruption for moderate disease, and admission with high dose parenteral corticosteroid for severe disease, escalating to infliximab or vedolizumab if there is no response within about three days. Infection must always be excluded first because the treatments diverge completely, and a steroid taper of at least four to six weeks is needed since rapid withdrawal produces relapse. The other immune related toxicities to consider in any unwell patient on these agents are hypophysitis, thyroid dysfunction, adrenal insufficiency, hepatitis, pneumonitis, nephritis and myocarditis.
key_points: Exclude infection first, since treatment for colitis and for infection diverge entirely
Antimotility agents mask severity and are avoided in suspected immune colitis
Grade 3 colitis needs drug interruption and corticosteroid at 1 to 2 mg/kg
Escalate to infliximab or vedolizumab if no response within about three days
Taper corticosteroid over at least four to six weeks to prevent relapse
explanation.pearls: Immune related adverse events can appear months after the last dose because the drugs act on immune memory rather than persisting in the circulation, so a patient who stopped pembrolizumab three months ago and presents with bloody diarrhoea still has immune colitis high on the differential.

subtopic_detail: Jaundice and a tender enlarged liver three weeks after a heavy drinking period with a bilirubin of 280 and an international normalised ratio of 1.9
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 47 year old man who has become progressively jaundiced over three weeks following several months of drinking around 20 standard drinks daily. He stopped drinking eight days ago.

He has anorexia and a dull ache under the right ribs. His vital signs are pulse 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in air and temperature 37.8 degrees Celsius. He is deeply jaundiced with a smooth tender liver palpable 4 cm below the costal margin and mild ascites. He is fully oriented with no asterixis. His bilirubin is 280 micromol/L (less than 20), aspartate aminotransferase is 186 U/L (less than 40), alanine aminotransferase is 74 U/L (less than 40), international normalised ratio is 1.9, creatinine is 88 micromol/L and white cell count is 14.2 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0). His chest radiograph is clear, blood and urine cultures are negative at 48 hours, an ascitic tap shows 120 neutrophils per mm3, and viral hepatitis serology and autoimmune markers are negative. His abdominal ultrasound with Doppler shows a coarse echotexture with patent hepatic and portal veins and no biliary dilatation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in air, temperature 37.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Deep jaundice, smooth tender liver edge 4 cm below the costal margin, mild ascites with shifting dullness, spider naevi over the upper chest, fully oriented with no asterixis, Glasgow Coma Scale 15
data_table.Investigations: Bilirubin 280 micromol/L (less than 20), aspartate aminotransferase 186 U/L (less than 40), alanine aminotransferase 74 U/L (less than 40), alkaline phosphatase 168 U/L (30 to 110), albumin 26 g/L (35 to 50), international normalised ratio 1.9, creatinine 88 micromol/L (60 to 110), white cell count 14.2 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), platelets 118 x10^9/L (150 to 400), ascitic fluid 120 neutrophils per mm3 with negative culture, blood and urine cultures negative at 48 hours, chest radiograph clear, hepatitis A B C and E serology negative, antinuclear and anti smooth muscle antibodies negative, ultrasound with Doppler showing coarse hepatic echotexture with patent hepatic and portal veins and no biliary dilatation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Give a 21 hour N-acetylcysteine infusion and monitor liver function
options.rationale: N-acetylcysteine treats paracetamol hepatotoxicity, which produces transaminases in the thousands with a relatively low bilirubin early on, the opposite of this pattern of modest transaminases with deep jaundice. There is no history of paracetamol ingestion here. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Alcohol related liver disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Alcohol related liver disease

options.text: Start prednisolone 40 mg daily with nutritional support and thiamine
options.rationale: Jaundice developing within weeks of heavy drinking with an aspartate to alanine aminotransferase ratio above 2, a bilirubin of 280 micromol/L and an international normalised ratio of 1.9 indicates severe alcohol related hepatitis, and prednisolone 40 mg daily is indicated at this severity once sepsis and gastrointestinal bleeding have been excluded, alongside intensive nutritional support, thiamine and abstinence. Response is assessed at day 7 using the Lille score, and corticosteroid is stopped in non-responders because continuing it adds infection risk without benefit. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Alcohol related liver disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Alcohol related liver disease

options.text: Start intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily for bacterial peritonitis
options.rationale: That diagnosis requires an ascitic neutrophil count of 250 per mm3 or more, and his count is 120 with negative cultures, so the threshold is not met. The raised white cell count and low grade fever are themselves features of the inflammatory syndrome rather than proof of infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange urgent transjugular liver biopsy before considering any treatment
options.rationale: Biopsy is not required when the clinical and biochemical picture is characteristic and competing causes have been excluded serologically and on imaging, and delaying treatment for it costs time in a condition with high short term mortality. Transjugular biopsy is reserved for genuine diagnostic uncertainty, particularly where an alternative cause remains plausible. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Alcohol related liver disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Alcohol related liver disease

options.text: Give lactulose 30 mL three times daily and restrict dietary protein
options.rationale: Treatment for hepatic encephalopathy is not indicated in a patient who is fully oriented with no asterixis, and protein restriction is now specifically discouraged in liver disease because it worsens the sarcopenia that drives poor outcomes. Adequate protein intake of around 1.2 to 1.5 g/kg daily is part of correct management. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Alcohol related liver disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Alcohol related liver disease

explanation.summary: Alcohol related hepatitis is a distinct syndrome of acute hepatic inflammation superimposed on chronic alcohol use, presenting with jaundice developing over weeks in someone drinking heavily up to or close to presentation, and it carries a short term mortality of up to 30 to 50 per cent in its severe form. The biochemical signature is a modest transaminase rise with an aspartate to alanine aminotransferase ratio above 2 alongside a disproportionately high bilirubin and a prolonged international normalised ratio, which differentiates it from viral and ischaemic hepatitis and from paracetamol toxicity where transaminases dominate. Severity is quantified using the Maddrey discriminant function or the model for end stage liver disease, and severe disease is the group in whom corticosteroid is considered, with prednisolone 40 mg daily conferring a modest short term survival benefit provided sepsis, active gastrointestinal bleeding and uncontrolled renal failure have been excluded. Response is formally reassessed at day 7 with the Lille score so that non-responders can be spared further immunosuppression. The interventions that matter most across the whole cohort are aggressive nutritional support with adequate protein and thiamine, vigilance for infection and acute kidney injury, and sustained abstinence with addiction support, since abstinence determines long term survival far more than any drug.
key_points: Aspartate to alanine aminotransferase ratio above 2 with deep jaundice is the signature
Severity scores identify the minority who may benefit from corticosteroid
Exclude sepsis and gastrointestinal bleeding before starting corticosteroid
Reassess response at day 7 and stop steroid in non-responders
Protein restriction is harmful; nutrition and abstinence drive long term outcome
explanation.pearls: An ascitic neutrophil count of 250 per mm3 is the threshold for treating spontaneous bacterial peritonitis regardless of culture result, so a count of 120 does not warrant antibiotics while a count of 300 with a sterile culture does.

subtopic_detail: Morning confusion relieved by orange juice with a glucose of 2.1, raised insulin and C-peptide and a negative sulfonylurea screen
stem:
You are the general physician seeing a 39 year old woman with six months of episodes in which she becomes confused, sweaty and tremulous, mostly before breakfast or if a meal is delayed. Her husband says she becomes vague and cannot follow a conversation, and that a glass of orange juice reverses it within minutes.

She has gained 7 kg because she now eats every two hours to prevent episodes. She has no diabetes, works as a florist, and no one in the household has diabetes or access to insulin or tablets for it. During a supervised 72 hour fast she became symptomatic at 14 hours with a plasma glucose of 2.1 mmol/L. Samples taken at that moment show insulin inappropriately detectable, C-peptide raised, proinsulin raised and beta hydroxybutyrate suppressed. Her sulfonylurea and meglitinide screen is negative, her morning cortisol is within normal limits and her insulin antibodies are negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits between episodes
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 29 kg/m2, no hyperpigmentation, no hepatomegaly, no abdominal mass, normal neurological examination between episodes, no lipohypertrophy or injection sites
data_table.Investigations: At the point of symptomatic hypoglycaemia during supervised fasting: plasma glucose 2.1 mmol/L (3.5 to 7.8), insulin inappropriately detectable, C-peptide raised, proinsulin raised, beta hydroxybutyrate suppressed; sulfonylurea and meglitinide screen negative; insulin antibodies negative; morning cortisol within normal limits; short synacthen test normal; liver function tests and creatinine within normal limits; HbA1c 4.7 per cent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Reassure her and advise frequent small meals with a bedtime snack
options.rationale: Dietary measures are what she is already doing and they have produced weight gain without preventing episodes, and reassurance is unsafe once fasting hypoglycaemia with inappropriate insulin secretion has been documented. Frequent meals are appropriate for postprandial reactive symptoms with normal fasting studies. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start diazoxide and review her symptom diary again in three months
options.rationale: Agents that suppress insulin secretion such as diazoxide are used for symptom control in patients whose lesion cannot be localised or who are unfit for surgery, not as an alternative to establishing the anatomy in a fit 39 year old. Medical therapy also leaves a potentially malignant lesion in place. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Measure insulin like growth factor 2 and screen for an occult malignancy
options.rationale: Non-islet cell tumour hypoglycaemia is mediated by incompletely processed insulin like growth factor 2 and characteristically suppresses insulin, C-peptide and proinsulin rather than raising them. Her raised C-peptide and proinsulin establish that the hypoglycaemia is insulin mediated and exclude that mechanism. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Arrange pancreatic imaging to localise the lesion for surgical resection
options.rationale: Endogenous hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia is established by a raised insulin, C-peptide and proinsulin with suppressed ketones at a glucose of 2.1 mmol/L and a negative sulfonylurea screen, which points to an insulinoma, so the next step is localisation with pancreatic protocol computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging, adding endoscopic ultrasound or somatostatin receptor imaging when cross sectional imaging is negative. Surgical enucleation or resection is curative in the great majority, and screening for multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 is considered given her age. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Begin hydrocortisone replacement for probable adrenal insufficiency
options.rationale: Adrenal insufficiency causes hypoglycaemia by loss of counter-regulation and would show a suppressed insulin and C-peptide with an inadequate cortisol response, whereas her morning cortisol and short synacthen test are both normal. Treating a normal adrenal axis would add iatrogenic harm without addressing the insulin excess. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Hypoglycaemia in a person without diabetes is investigated by documenting Whipple triad, symptoms with a low plasma glucose relieved by correcting it, and then by taking a critical sample at the moment of hypoglycaemia, because a normal insulin measured when the glucose is normal is uninterpretable. That sample sorts the differential decisively: insulin mediated hypoglycaemia shows detectable insulin with suppressed ketones, and within that group a raised C-peptide indicates endogenous secretion from an insulinoma, nesidioblastosis or a sulfonylurea, while a suppressed C-peptide indicates exogenous insulin administration. A drug screen therefore matters as much as the hormone panel, since surreptitious or accidental sulfonylurea exposure exactly mimics an insulinoma biochemically, while non-islet cell tumour hypoglycaemia mediated by insulin like growth factor 2 and counter-regulatory failure from adrenal insufficiency both suppress all the insulin related measures. Once endogenous hyperinsulinism is established, localisation precedes surgery, which cures most patients, and around 5 to 10 per cent of insulinomas arise in multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1, where lesions are multiple and younger patients are affected.
key_points: The critical sample must be taken at the moment of documented hypoglycaemia
Detectable insulin with suppressed ketones indicates insulin mediated hypoglycaemia
Raised C-peptide means endogenous secretion; suppressed means exogenous insulin
A sulfonylurea screen is essential because it mimics insulinoma exactly
Around 5 to 10 per cent of insulinomas occur in multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1
explanation.pearls: Proinsulin is the measure that most reliably separates an insulinoma from a sulfonylurea effect, because tumour cells secrete incompletely processed hormone and proinsulin is disproportionately raised, whereas a sulfonylurea drives release of normally processed insulin from healthy beta cells.
