subtopic_detail: Creatinine rising from 98 to 186 ten days after perindopril was started in a smoker with bruits over both flanks
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 71 year old man referred by his general practitioner because of a rise in creatinine. He has hypertension that has needed four agents to control, peripheral vascular disease with bilateral calf claudication, and a 50 pack year smoking history.

Ten days ago perindopril was added because his blood pressure remained at 168/94 mmHg despite amlodipine, hydrochlorothiazide and prazosin. He feels well and has not had diarrhoea, vomiting or reduced oral intake, and takes no non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. On examination he is not volume depleted, with a jugular venous pressure visible at 2 cm and no postural drop, and there are audible bruits over both flanks and absent foot pulses. His creatinine has risen from 98 to 186 micromol/L with potassium 5.4 mmol/L, and his urinalysis shows no blood, no protein and no casts. Renal ultrasound reports a right kidney of 11.2 cm and a left kidney of 8.4 cm with increased cortical echogenicity on the left.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 156/90 mmHg with no postural drop, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Jugular venous pressure visible at 2 cm with no postural blood pressure drop, chest clear, audible bruits over both flanks, absent dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses bilaterally, no peripheral oedema, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 186 micromol/L, up from 98 micromol/L four weeks ago (60 to 110), potassium 5.4 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), sodium 138 mmol/L (135 to 145), bicarbonate 21 mmol/L (22 to 32), urinalysis showing no blood, no protein and no casts, renal ultrasound with a right kidney 11.2 cm and left kidney 8.4 cm with increased left cortical echogenicity, full blood count within normal limits, C reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Give intravenous fluids for presumed prerenal acute kidney injury
options.rationale: He is clinically euvolaemic with a visible jugular venous pressure, no postural drop and no history of fluid loss, so there is no volume deficit to replace and fluid loading risks pulmonary oedema. Volume expansion is the right answer when history and examination indicate depletion. (Source: KHA-CARI: Acute kidney injury guidance)

options.text: Stop the perindopril and arrange imaging of the renal arteries
options.rationale: A sharp creatinine rise within two weeks of starting renin angiotensin blockade in a vasculopath with resistant hypertension, flank bruits and asymmetric kidney sizes points to critical renal artery stenosis, in which glomerular filtration depends on angiotensin mediated efferent arteriolar tone, so the drug is withdrawn and the anatomy defined with computed tomography or magnetic resonance angiography. Bland urinalysis excludes an intrinsic glomerular or interstitial process and supports a haemodynamic mechanism. (Source: KHA-CARI: Acute kidney injury guidance)

options.text: Continue the perindopril and repeat his biochemistry in four weeks
options.rationale: A rise of up to about 30 per cent in creatinine after starting renin angiotensin blockade is expected and acceptable, but his creatinine has risen by 90 per cent with hyperkalaemia, which exceeds that threshold and requires action. Watchful continuation applies to the smaller expected rise. (Source: KHA-CARI: Acute kidney injury guidance)

options.text: Start high dose prednisolone for probable acute interstitial nephritis
options.rationale: Interstitial nephritis typically produces white cells, white cell casts or eosinophils in the urine, often with rash and eosinophilia, and his urinalysis is entirely bland with a normal C reactive protein. Corticosteroid would add harm without treating the haemodynamic cause. (Source: KHA-CARI: Acute kidney injury guidance)

options.text: Refer for renal biopsy to establish the cause before changing his drugs
options.rationale: Biopsy is invasive and carries bleeding risk, and it is not needed when a clear temporal drug association and supportive imaging explain the picture. It becomes appropriate where the urinalysis is active, an intrinsic renal disease is suspected and function does not recover after removing the precipitant. (Source: KHA-CARI: Acute kidney injury guidance)

explanation.summary: Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors and receptor blockers reduce intraglomerular pressure by dilating the efferent arteriole, which is precisely why they protect the kidney in proteinuric disease and also why they precipitate a functional fall in filtration where perfusion pressure is already critically dependent on that tone. A creatinine rise of up to around 30 per cent after initiation is expected, is not a reason to stop, and is associated with better long term outcomes, but a larger or progressive rise with hyperkalaemia signals that the drug has unmasked a haemodynamically significant lesion. Atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis is the classic cause and should be suspected in an older vasculopath with resistant hypertension, asymmetric kidney sizes, flank bruits, recurrent flash pulmonary oedema or a bland urinalysis alongside the creatinine rise. Diagnosis is by computed tomography or magnetic resonance angiography, and the important therapeutic nuance is that randomised trials have not shown revascularisation to be better than optimal medical therapy for most patients, so stenting is reserved for those with refractory hypertension despite maximal treatment, progressive renal impairment, recurrent pulmonary oedema or stenosis affecting a solitary functioning kidney.
key_points: A creatinine rise up to about 30 per cent after starting the drug is expected
A larger rise with hyperkalaemia suggests a critical perfusion dependent lesion
Bland urinalysis separates a haemodynamic cause from intrinsic renal disease
Asymmetric kidney size, flank bruits and resistant hypertension support the diagnosis
Revascularisation is reserved for refractory cases, not offered routinely
explanation.pearls: Recurrent flash pulmonary oedema with preserved left ventricular function in a hypertensive vasculopath is the presentation most specific for bilateral renal artery stenosis, and it is one of the few indications where revascularisation clearly outperforms medical therapy.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Renal artery stenosis

subtopic_detail: Ringing ears, deep rapid breathing and agitation after a large ingestion of tablets for arthritis, with a pH of 7.44 and a bicarbonate of 12
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 34 year old woman brought in four hours after taking an unknown number of tablets from a bottle of her mother's arthritis medication. She is agitated, complains of ringing in her ears and says she feels hot.

Her vital signs are pulse 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in air and temperature 38.2 degrees Celsius. She is breathing deeply and is diaphoretic, restless and confused but rousable with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 14, and she has no focal neurological signs. Her arterial blood gas shows pH 7.44, partial pressure of carbon dioxide 18 mmHg, bicarbonate 12 mmol/L and lactate 2.6 mmol/L. Her sodium is 140 mmol/L, potassium 3.2 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, glucose 4.6 mmol/L and creatinine 96 micromol/L. Her paracetamol level is undetectable and her salicylate level is 720 mg/L (therapeutic 150 to 300), rising from 640 mg/L an hour earlier.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 38.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Agitated and confused but rousable with Glasgow Coma Scale 14, deep rapid respiration, diaphoretic with warm peripheries, tinnitus reported, no focal neurological deficit, pupils equal and reactive, no clonus or rigidity
data_table.Investigations: Arterial blood gas pH 7.44, partial pressure of carbon dioxide 18 mmHg, bicarbonate 12 mmol/L, lactate 2.6 mmol/L; sodium 140 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), chloride 102 mmol/L (95 to 110), bicarbonate 12 mmol/L (22 to 32), glucose 4.6 mmol/L (3.5 to 7.8), creatinine 96 micromol/L (45 to 90); salicylate 720 mg/L rising from 640 mg/L one hour earlier (therapeutic 150 to 300); paracetamol undetectable; electrocardiogram showing sinus tachycardia with a QTc of 420 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Intubate and ventilate her now to protect the airway given her confusion
options.rationale: Intubation is the most dangerous intervention available here, because paralysis removes the compensatory hyperventilation that is maintaining her pH and the resulting respiratory acidosis drives salicylate across the blood brain barrier, with cardiac arrest reported after induction. If ventilation becomes unavoidable, hyperventilation must be maintained and alkalinisation continued throughout. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give activated charcoal and repeat the salicylate level in four hours
options.rationale: Activated charcoal has a genuine role and may be given even at this interval because salicylate delays gastric emptying and can form concretions, but it is wholly insufficient as the sole response to a rising level above 700 mg/L with confusion. Charcoal alone would be reasonable for an asymptomatic patient with a low and falling level. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Start intravenous sodium bicarbonate and defer dialysis until the pH falls
options.rationale: Alkalinisation is correct and urgent, but waiting for the pH to fall before referring for dialysis misreads the trajectory, since a normal or alkalotic pH in salicylate poisoning reflects intact respiratory compensation that fails abruptly as the patient tires. Deferring until acidaemia appears means intervening after deterioration rather than before it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Start sodium bicarbonate with potassium replacement and refer for dialysis
options.rationale: A salicylate level above 700 mg/L that is still rising, together with confusion, marks severe poisoning, so urinary alkalinisation with a sodium bicarbonate infusion is started immediately while the renal team is contacted for urgent haemodialysis, which clears salicylate and corrects the acid base disturbance. Potassium must be replaced aggressively because hypokalaemia prevents the kidney from excreting an alkaline urine, and the neurological features rather than the pH are what mandate extracorporeal removal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give intravenous fluids with active cooling and observe her in the department
options.rationale: Volume resuscitation and temperature control are supportive measures that accompany definitive treatment, and hyperthermia here reflects uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation rather than an infective or environmental cause. Observation without alkalinisation or dialysis in a confused patient with a rising level risks rapid deterioration to seizures and cardiac arrest. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: Salicylate poisoning produces a characteristic mixed acid base disturbance that is easy to misread: direct stimulation of the respiratory centre causes a primary respiratory alkalosis, while uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation and accumulation of organic acids produce a high anion gap metabolic acidosis, so the measured pH depends entirely on which process is currently winning. In this patient the anion gap is raised at 26 mmol/L while the pH remains 7.44, which means respiratory compensation is intact and is doing the work of keeping her alive; a normal pH is therefore reassuring only in the way that a normal blood pressure is reassuring in compensated shock. The clinical features that determine severity are neurological rather than biochemical, since confusion, agitation, seizures and coma indicate central nervous system salicylate penetration, which is promoted by acidaemia because only the non-ionised form crosses the blood brain barrier. This mechanism explains the two management principles that candidates most often get wrong: alkalinisation is given to trap salicylate in the extracellular space and the urine rather than simply to correct a number, and intubation is hazardous because paralysis abolishes the hyperventilation, acidaemia follows, and drug floods into the brain. Indications for haemodialysis are a level above roughly 700 mg/L, altered mental state, seizures, pulmonary oedema, renal impairment or refractory acidosis, and they are assessed on the trajectory rather than on a single value.
key_points: The disturbance is mixed respiratory alkalosis with high anion gap metabolic acidosis
A normal pH reflects intact compensation, not a mild poisoning
Neurological features rather than pH determine severity and dialysis need
Hypokalaemia prevents alkaline urine and must be corrected aggressively
Intubation removes compensatory hyperventilation and can precipitate arrest
explanation.pearls: Salicylate is a weak acid with a pKa near 3, so raising urine pH to between 7.5 and 8.5 converts it to the ionised form that cannot be reabsorbed by the renal tubule and increases elimination several fold; this cannot be achieved while the patient is hypokalaemic, because the distal tubule then exchanges potassium for hydrogen and acidifies the urine regardless of how much bicarbonate is infused.

sources.label: Australian Poisons Information Centre: Salicylate poisoning guidance
